docs.title: Neural Network
docs.text: Neural networks rely on two key mathematical processes: forward propagation (for predictions) and backward propagation (for learning via gradient descent).

docs.title: The Math Behind Neural Network Forward and Backward Propagation
docs.text: Neural networks rely on two key mathematical processes: forward propagation (for predictions) and backward propagation (for learning via gradient descent). In this post, we break down the core math behind these steps using a simple 3-layer neural network example. Hand-written calculations and diagrams from my notes are included for clarity.

docs.title: Network Architecture
docs.text:
We consider a neural network with:

  • Input layer: 3 neurons (x₁, x₂, x₃)
  • Hidden layer: 2 neurons (h₄, h₅)
  • Output layer: 1 neuron (o₆)
Input Layer (x₁, x₂, x₃) → Hidden Layer (h₄, h₅) → Output Layer (o₆)

docs.title: 1. Forward Pass
docs.text: The forward pass computes the output of each neuron layer-by-layer using weights (ω), biases (b), and activation functions (sigmoid here).

docs.title: Hidden Layer Calculations
docs.text:
For neuron 4 (h₄):

a4 = sigmoid(inputs * weights + b4)

From the notes:

a4 = 1 / (1 + exp(-(-0.7))) = 0.332

For neuron 5 (h₅):

a5 = 1 / (1 + exp(-0.1)) = 0.325

docs.title: Output Layer Calculation
docs.text:
o6 = sigmoid(a4 * ω46 + a5 * ω56 + b6)

a6 = 1 / (1 + exp(-(-0.206))) = 0.194

docs.title: 2. Loss Calculation
docs.text:
The error (loss) is computed between the prediction (o₆) and the target value.

From the notes (target = 1):

Error = 1 - 0.414 = 0.526

docs.title: 3. Backward Propagation
docs.text: Backward propagation applies the chain rule to compute gradients for each weight and bias.

docs.title: Output Neuron Gradient (δ₆)
docs.text:
δ6 = Error × sigmoid'(o6)

where

sigmoid'(z) = sigmoid(z) * (1 - sigmoid(z))

From the notes:

δ6 = 0.414 × (1 - 0.414) × (1 - 0.414) = 0.131

docs.title: 4. Weight Updates
docs.text:
Weights are updated using the computed gradients and a learning rate (η=0.9).

Update Rule:

Δωij = η × δi × aj
ωij_new = ωij_old + Δωij

Example Updates (see notes):

  • Weight ω16 (input 1 → output 6):

    Δω16 = 0.9 × 0.131 × 0.392 = 0.046
ω16_new = 0.939 - 0.3 = 0.639

  • Weight ω35 (input 3 → hidden 5):

    Δω35 = 0.9 × 0.00653 × 1 = 0.00588
ω35_new = 0.2 - 0.00857 = 0.19143

docs.title: 5. Bias Updates
docs.text:
Biases are updated similarly:

bi_new = bi_old + η × δi

For output neuron 6:

b6_new = 0.1 + (0.9 × 0.131) = 0.218

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text: Component Equation Forward Pass a_j = sigmoid(sum_over_i(ω_ij * x_i) + b_j) Sigmoid sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z)) Output Gradient δ_k = (y - y_hat) * sigmoid'(o_k) Hidden Gradient δ_j = sigmoid'(a_j) * sum_over_k(δ_k * ω_jk) Weight Update Δω_ij = η * δ_j * a_i Bias Update Δb_j = η * δ_j

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Backpropagation efficiently computes gradients by:

  1. Forward pass: Calculate predictions and cache values.
  2. Backward pass: Apply the chain rule for error gradients.
  3. Update: Adjust weights and biases to minimize loss.

Your files and these notes demonstrate a practical implementation of these principles—calculating gradients and updating weights. While the math may appear complex, it systematically optimizes the network using calculus and linear algebra.

docs.title: From Unboxing to Zero Day: Satellite Receiver Security Research
docs.text: When I first picked up a GX6607 based satellite receiver I had one question in mind. How secure is this thing? What followed was months of hardware hacking, firmware analysis, reverse engineering and live testing across several receivers. This post is the updated technical companion to my talks at XCon and SANS CyberThreat 2026 in London, including what I got wrong the first time around.

docs.title: What Changed Since the First Version of This Post
docs.text:
Research is iterative, and some of my early conclusions did not survive a second look. In the spirit of separating what is confirmed from what is inferred, here is what I corrected:

  • There were two firmware platforms, not one. The UART boot log and the CH341A flash dump came from an older eCos based receiver with a 4 MB SPI NOR chip. The GX6607 receiver, where I found the root shell, runs Linux from a 128 MB SPI NAND flash. Both appear in this post, and each section says which device it is about.
  • "JBOOT" and "Blowfish" were binwalk false positives. binwalk reported JBOOT headers (one claiming a 1.1 GB image inside a 10 MB file), ESP32 images and Blowfish encrypted regions. None of them were real. The boot log clearly names the bootloader as zeroBoot.
  • The boot log did not give me dvbapp's load address. dvbapp is an ELF file and carries its own base address. The addresses in the boot log belong to the eCos firmware.
  • The buffer overflow is confirmed in code, not exploited. I have not demonstrated a path that delivers attacker-controlled data to it, so I no longer assign it an attack vector.

docs.title: The Targets
docs.text:
The main target is a satellite set-top box built on the Nationalchip GX6607 SoC. It is sold at retail as the GAZAL BOSS S5 FOREVER, while its firmware identifies itself as GAZAL BOSS 03 FOREVER. That mismatch matters: it shows the same firmware is shared across models and brands. The box runs embedded Linux, and a single 10 MB ARM application called dvbapp handles almost everything: DVB reception, conditional access, IPTV, OTT apps, the user interface and network services.

I also tested older receivers from the same market, built in different years. One of them runs eCos, a real-time operating system, from a 4 MB SPI NOR chip. That box is where the UART and flash dumping work below took place.

docs.title: Opening the Device and Finding UART (eCos receiver)
docs.text:
The first step in any hardware engagement is getting eyes on the PCB. After removing the case I photographed the board and identified the SoC, the SPI flash in an SOIC8 package, the DDR memory and a set of test pads near the edge of the board.

I used a multimeter to profile each pad against ground while the device was powered. The TX line fluctuates during boot and then settles at 3.3 V. The RX line sits at 3.3 V waiting for input. Ground is ground.

The baud rate took longer. My first logic analyzer capture at 20 kHz showed what looked like a clean clock signal. The problem was my setup, not the device: 20 kHz is far too slow to resolve any standard baud rate above 2400. After recapturing at 4 MHz the pulses had the variable widths of real UART framing, and I calculated the baud rate from the shortest pulse in PulseView.

The second lesson was about terminal software. Minicom is forgiving about baud rate mismatches and can show plausible text at the wrong rate. Picocom is strict. If minicom looks clean but picocom shows garbage, your baud rate is wrong. Verify with the strict tool before trusting what you see.

docs.title: What the Boot Log Gave Away
docs.text:
Power cycling the board produced a complete boot log. In about ten seconds the device told me:

zeroBoot v1.0 for 1506F
SPI SCS flow
jump to second boot!!
Boot form SPI v1.11
DRAM-512M
copy fw to RAM
1ST BOOT
LD eCos v1.16 1506f
20111226-V1.1, RAM_START:=0x81600000
file:system_others.c,line176: LZMA Unzip module m_info.lma:=0x1b924,m_info.lma_size:=0x83a41
file:system_others.c,line213: bootloader m_info.vma:=0x80010000
SQMACSQMAC
XCAS_V21.09.01
ISH_V21.09.01
  • The boot chain: a zeroBoot first stage, a second stage from SPI flash, then eCos.
  • Factory debug output left on: pages of DDR calibration registers, source file names and line numbers, printed on every boot of a consumer product.
  • No visible integrity check: nothing in the boot chain reports a signature or integrity verification before handing over to the next stage.
  • Old code: the loader version string is dated 26 December 2011.
  • Instructions for reverse engineering: the log states where the compressed application sits in flash, how large it is, and the address it is loaded to. That is exactly what you need to extract it and load it into Ghidra correctly.
  • Card sharing modules load at boot: the conditional access and softcam modules are part of the boot sequence, not an add-on.

docs.title: Dumping the Firmware (eCos receiver)
docs.text:
The CH341A programmer with an SOIC8 clip read the 4 MB GigaDevice SPI NOR chip without trouble once I followed three rules: the board must be fully powered off, the programmer must use 3.3 V logic, and a short, good quality USB cable avoids the brownouts that make the CH341A disconnect mid-read.

I always take three reads and compare their hashes. If they differ, the clip connection is unreliable and anything you analyse is meaningless.

The channel database was readable in plain text and listed transponders for Nilesat, Badr, Hotbird, Astra and dozens more, which reveals the market the device was built for. The dump also held cached runtime data, including Wi-Fi credentials from whoever configured the device before me. If you sell or repair one of these boxes without wiping it, your home network password goes with it.

docs.title: A Lesson About Trusting Tools
docs.text: My first pass leaned heavily on binwalk's signature scan, and I reported what it said: JBOOT headers, Blowfish encrypted regions, ESP32 images. On review, these were false positives. Short magic-number signatures match random bytes in large binaries all the time. Treat binwalk's output as a list of leads to verify, never as findings.

docs.title: Getting Inside the GX6607 (Linux receiver)
docs.text: The GX6607 box took a very different path. A network scan showed telnet open on port 23.

docs.title: The Critical Finding: Root Without a Password
docs.text:
Connecting to port 23 gives a root shell immediately. There is no login prompt. The cause is two lines in the read-only system image:

  • The init script starts telnetd with a custom login program, /etc/autologin.
  • That script simply runs login -f root, which logs in as root without checking a password.

On top of that, the root account in /etc/passwd has no password at all.

Because this lives in the read-only squashfs image, it is not a leftover setting a user could change. It was built into the firmware.

From this shell an attacker can read every credential stored on the device, harvest its configuration, watch its traffic, and use it as a foothold into the rest of the home network.

  • CWE: CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for Critical Function), CWE-1188 (Insecure Default Initialization), CWE-912 (Hidden Functionality)
  • CVSS 3.1: 9.6 Critical (AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) for a typical home network. If the device is directly reachable from the internet, for example through a cellular connection with a public IP, the attack vector becomes network and the score 10.0.

docs.title: A Second Unauthenticated Service
docs.text: dvbapp also runs an HTTP service on a local network port. That service returns files from the device's filesystem to anyone who asks, with no authentication. It is independent of telnet, so it remains exposed even if telnet were disabled. I have included it in my disclosure.

docs.title: What Is Listening
docs.text: dvbapp alone listens on six TCP ports. telnetd listens on every interface, IPv4 and IPv6. Every way the box connects to a network (Ethernet, Wi-Fi or cellular) leads to the same root shell.

docs.title: Static Analysis in Ghidra (dvbapp)
docs.text:
dvbapp is a 32-bit little-endian ARM ELF. Ghidra picks up its base address from the ELF headers, which matched the process memory map on the running device. With the Function Start Search and Aggressive Instruction Finder analysers enabled, Ghidra recovered most of the function structure without symbols.

My approach is strings first. A distinctive string is an anchor: find it, follow its cross-references to the function that uses it, and work outward.

docs.title: Hardcoded Authentication Secrets
docs.text:
The IPTV service dispatcher builds an authentication token for its backend API by hashing a secret salt together with the device's MAC address, serial number and model name. The salt is hardcoded in the binary. A second hardcoded key is used by the request builder for another IPTV service.

Anyone who extracts these secrets can generate valid tokens for any device whose identifiers they know, without a subscription. I have deliberately left the values and the exact token format out of this post.

  • CWE: CWE-798 (Use of Hard-coded Credentials), CWE-321 (Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key)
  • CVSS 3.1: 7.5 High

docs.title: A Stack Buffer Overflow, Confirmed in Code Only
docs.text:
One small function copies a caller-supplied number of bytes into a fixed 260-byte stack buffer with no bounds check, then passes the buffer to a hardware write routine. The code around its callers checks an XOR checksum and a status word typical of smartcard communication, so it appears to be part of the conditional access path.

This is a real coding flaw (CWE-121). However, the callers I traced pass small fixed or byte-bounded lengths, and I have not shown a way for outside data to reach it with an oversized length. I therefore report it as a code-quality finding without an attack vector or exploitability claim.

docs.title: No Memory Protections
docs.text: The process memory map shows every region of dvbapp, including the stack and heap, as readable, writable and executable. There is no ASLR, no stack canaries and no NX. These protections are standard on modern Linux, and their absence turns any memory corruption bug into a far more serious problem.

docs.title: A Correction: The Broadcast Parser Bug That Was Not
docs.text: Earlier I suspected an unchecked index in what I took for a DVB broadcast table parser. A closer look showed the structure holds IPTV stream records, not broadcast tables, and the index is range-checked before use. I have dropped that finding.

docs.title: What They Left Behind
docs.text:
Live inspection of the GX6607 turned up a long trail of development and configuration leftovers:

  • Developer artefacts: build paths naming individual developers, a developer's Wi-Fi network credentials, and a debug script that mounts a development server over NFS.
  • A hardcoded Wi-Fi hotspot configuration with a weak, guessable default passphrase.
  • A preloaded cellular database: 101 carrier profiles for USB 3G/4G modems across more than 20 countries, including Jordan's operators. These are public APN defaults, not leaked secrets, but they show cellular support is built in.
  • Chinese DNS by design: the cellular dialer scripts, credited to two named developers, deliberately keep a resolver configuration pointing at China Telecom (CHINANET) DNS servers after a cellular link comes up. A comment in the script says so explicitly. On that path, every domain the box looks up goes to those servers.
  • A default China Telecom CDMA login left over from the reference design.
  • A boot video from a writable partition. At every boot, a root process opens a video file from a writable flash partition, and a companion file suggests that video can be downloaded from a remote URL. Whoever controls that content controls what a media parser running as root opens at boot. This is an attack surface I have not yet tested.
  • A leftover OpenVPN DNS file, but no VPN client and no code in dvbapp that uses one. I mention it only so nobody overreads it.

docs.title: Assessing the RF Attack Surface
docs.text:
Assessing RF does not start with a transmitter. It starts with knowing which radios the box has, how each one works, and where each one leads.

Radio How it works on this box Status Satellite (DVB-S/S2) Tuner → hardware demux → descrambler. The kernel also ships IP-over-satellite encapsulation paths (GSE, ULE). Observed Wi-Fi USB Wi-Fi/Bluetooth combo chip in client mode, plus a shipped hotspot configuration Configuration confirmed Wi-Fi Direct A p2p0 interface and a screen-mirroring (Wi-Fi Display) module Inferred from names Bluetooth LE Used by the remote control Observed Cellular USB 3G/4G modem support with PPP dialer scripts Configuration confirmed

Three conclusions follow:

  1. The broadcast signal is not authenticated. Anyone who can transmit on the right frequency is talking to the box's parsers.
  2. The decryption keys come from the internet, not from a smartcard (see the next section).
  3. Every radio leads to the same root shell, because telnet listens on every interface.

docs.title: IKS: Card Sharing Built Into the Firmware
docs.text:
Legitimate pay-TV works like this. Each channel is scrambled with a key that changes every few seconds. That key is broadcast in encrypted form, and only the subscriber's smartcard can decrypt it.

IKS (Internet Key Sharing) replaces the smartcard with a server on the internet. The receiver sends the encrypted key message to a server that holds a genuine subscription card and gets the decrypted key back. The video itself still comes from the dish; only a few bytes cross the internet.

On the GX6607 I confirmed:

  • Live, persistent connections to card-sharing servers. One is hosted in the Netherlands on infrastructure registered through a Belize entity.
  • The card-sharing protocols (CCcam, Newcamd, MGcamd and OSCam related code) built into dvbapp.
  • Device identification at activation: the activation request sends the device's MAC address and serial number to the operator.
  • No smartcard in use: decryption keys come only from the internet.

Why this matters for security:

  • The box keeps a permanent, encrypted, outbound connection to anonymous operators running illegal infrastructure.
  • dvbapp, running as root with no memory protections, parses everything those servers send back.
  • The operators know exactly which device is which.

Card sharing is illegal in many countries, including the UK. I document the infrastructure as evidence and do not use or demonstrate the service.

docs.title: From Vulnerable Box to Residential Proxy
docs.text:
In July 2026 the FBI and IRS-CI seized the domains of NetNut, a residential proxy service run by the Nasdaq-listed Israeli firm Alarum, together with Google, Lumen and Shadowserver. Researchers had linked NetNut to "Popa", a botnet of at least two million smart TVs and TV streaming boxes. These devices either shipped with proxy software or picked it up through apps, and customers rented their home internet connections. In a single week Google observed 316 distinct threat actor groups using NetNut exit nodes, including criminal and espionage groups. Alarum rejects the botnet label and says its software is consent-based.

I did not find any proxy software on the GX6607, and I am not claiming it is part of NetNut. But it fits the profile almost perfectly:

  • always on, behind a residential IP;
  • root with no password, on every interface;
  • already in contact with unknown servers by design;
  • nobody monitors it and nobody patches it.

It is not a botnet today. It is a ready-made node for one.

docs.title: How These Devices Get Into Homes
docs.text:
• Diaspora demand. Communities abroad want the channels they grew up with, so these receivers travel with them to Europe and North America. The users are the victims, not the threat.
  • Local label, foreign build. The boxes I bought say "Made in Jordan". Inside are a Chinese chipset, Chinese developer build paths and Chinese DNS servers. I expect the same pattern in other markets.
  • Borders check paperwork, not firmware. Customs checks duties and origin, and radio regulators check frequencies. Nobody inspects the code.
  • Nobody's job. It is not a computer, so IT does not own it. It is not a phone, so telecom security does not look at it.

docs.title: Responsible Disclosure
docs.text: I attempted to notify the vendors and distributors before publishing and have not received a response. A CVE request has been filed for the unauthenticated root shell. The findings were presented at XCon and will be presented at SANS CyberThreat 2026 in London on 17 November 2026. Secrets, credentials and step-by-step exploitation details are withheld from all public material.

docs.title: Lessons Learned
docs.text:
• Sample rate matters. Too low a sample rate does not give you garbage. It gives you plausible output that is completely wrong. Confirm with a strict tool.
  • Know which device a result came from. I mixed evidence from two platforms early on, and it led me to wrong conclusions. Label every artefact with its source.
  • Verify every tool's output. binwalk signatures, decompiler output and string matches are leads, not findings.
  • The boot log is a gift, when it belongs to the firmware you are analysing.
  • Separate confirmed, observed and inferred. It makes every claim you keep stronger.
  • The worst bug was the simplest. The most severe finding needed no firmware knowledge, no UART and no flash dump. It needed one telnet command.

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
Hardware: a CH341A programmer with an SOIC8 clip, a 3.3 V USB-to-UART adapter, a logic analyzer with PulseView, a multimeter, and an RTL-SDR for passive spectrum observation.

Software: flashrom, binwalk, Ghidra, picocom and minicom, standard Linux tools on the device itself, and public WHOIS, DNS and RIPE data for infrastructure research.

docs.text:

  • 'Popa' Botnet Linked to Publicly-Traded Israeli Firm (KrebsOnSecurity)
  • Google's Continued Disruption of Malicious Residential Proxy Networks (Google Threat Intelligence Group)

docs.title: SNR Blog
docs.text: Welcome to the blog for the Wi-Fi Proximity Sensor project, where we transform a standard Wi-Fi adapter into a real-time proximity detector using machine learning.

docs.title: Wi-Fi Proximity Sensor with Machine Learning: A Hacker's Guide
docs.text:
Hey hackers and pentesters! Want to turn a cheap Wi-Fi adapter into a stealthy proximity sensor for physical security assessments or red team ops? This Python-based project leverages wireless signal metrics—signal strength, noise level, and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)—to estimate distances to nearby objects or people. Whether you're detecting movement in a target environment, building covert presence detection, or integrating with IoT for sneaky automation, this tool has you covered. It combines raw signal processing with a machine learning pipeline for precision and adaptability.

The full source code will drop soon on GitHub (link coming soon).

docs.title: Project Overview
docs.text:
This Wi-Fi Proximity Sensor runs on Linux, sniffing metrics from a Wi-Fi interface to estimate proximity. It supports two modes: static threshold-based detection for quick setups, and a machine learning mode that trains on custom data for environment-specific accuracy. Built with Python 3, scikit-learn, and joblib, it uses system tools (iw, /proc/net/wireless, iwconfig) to pull raw signal data.

For pentesters, this is a lightweight, hackable tool for: - Physical security testing - Rogue device detection - Social engineering ops where proximity matters

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Metric Sniffing: Pulls signal strength and noise using multiple Linux tools for reliability across setups.
  • Proximity Estimation: Maps SNR to proximity zones ("Very Close," "Normal Range," "Moving Away," "Far Away") or exact distances via ML.
  • Signal Smoothing: Uses exponential moving average (EMA) to stabilize noisy Wi-Fi signals.
  • Machine Learning: Collects data and trains regression (LinearRegression) or classification (SVC) models for custom environments.
  • Real-Time Monitoring: Low-latency updates for dynamic scenarios like tailgating detection.
  • Pentesting Applications: Think intrusion detection, physical access monitoring, or IoT exploitation.

docs.title: Technical Breakdown
docs.text:
The system is built for hackers who love to tinker. It operates in four modes:

  1. Monitoring Mode: Real-time tracking of Wi-Fi metrics with proximity estimates using static thresholds or a trained model.
  2. Data Collection Mode: Logs signal data with ground-truth distances or labels for training custom models.
  3. Model Training Mode: Builds a scikit-learn pipeline to predict distances or proximity zones.
  4. Inference Mode: Deploys the trained model for live, environment-tuned proximity detection.

docs.title: Signal Processing
docs.text:
The system scrapes Wi-Fi metrics using a tiered approach to handle diverse hardware:

  • iw dev <interface> link: Modern, clean way to get signal strength (dBm).
  • /proc/net/wireless: Kernel-level stats for signal and noise, great for older systems.
  • iwconfig: Fallback for legacy setups, parsing signal/noise from text output.

SNR Calculation:

SNR = Signal Strength (dBm) - Noise Level (dBm)

If noise is unavailable (common in some adapters), it approximates:

SNR ≈ Signal Strength + 90

Signal Smoothing (EMA, α = 0.7):

SNR_smoothed_t = α · SNR_smoothed_{t-1} + (1-α) · SNR_raw_t

This keeps readings stable for reliable proximity estimates during pentests.

docs.title: Machine Learning Pipeline
docs.text:
For hackers, the ML component is where things get juicy. Feature vector includes:

  • Signal strength (dBm, default -100 if missing)
  • Noise level (dBm, default -90 if missing)
  • Smoothed SNR (dB, default 0 if missing)

The system auto-detects label type:

  • Regression (LinearRegression): Predicts distance (cm), mapped to zones:
  • <50 cm: "VERY CLOSE"
  • 50–200 cm: "NORMAL RANGE"
  • 200–400 cm: "MOVING AWAY"

  • 400 cm: "FAR AWAY"

  • Classification (SVC with probability): Directly predicts proximity zones.

A StandardScaler normalizes features to handle varying signal ranges. Models are serialized with joblib for quick deployment.

Pentesters can train models in specific environments (e.g., target office) to account for walls, interference, or hardware quirks.

docs.title: Pentesting Applications
docs.text:
• Physical Intrusion Detection: Detect tailgating or unauthorized access by monitoring SNR changes near doors or secure areas.
  • Rogue Device Tracking: Identify movement of Wi-Fi-enabled devices (e.g., laptops, phones) in restricted zones.
  • IoT Exploitation: Integrate with MQTT or Home Assistant to trigger payloads when someone approaches.
  • Social Engineering: Use proximity data to time physical access attempts or device interactions.

docs.title: Core Code (Preview)
docs.text:
Here’s a stripped-down version of the core logic, focusing on metric extraction and monitoring. The full code, with data collection and training, will be released soon.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import subprocess
import re
import time
import joblib
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

INTERFACE = "wlan0"
SAMPLING_RATE = 0.5
SMOOTHING_FACTOR = 0.7
MODEL_FILE = "wifi_proximity_model.pkl"

def get_wireless_metrics(interface):
    metrics = {'signal': None, 'noise': None}
    try:
        output = subprocess.check_output(["iw", "dev", interface, "link"], text=True, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
        sig_match = re.search(r"signal:\s*(-?\d+)\s*dBm", output)
        if sig_match:
            metrics['signal'] = int(sig_match.group(1))
    except Exception:
        try:
            with open("/proc/net/wireless", "r") as f:
                for line in f.readlines()[2:]:
                    if interface in line:
                        parts = line.strip().split()
                        if len(parts) >= 5:
                            metrics['signal'] = int(float(parts[3]))
                            metrics['noise'] = int(float(parts[4]))
                            break
        except Exception:
            pass
    return metrics

def calculate_snr(metrics):
    if metrics['signal'] is not None and metrics['noise'] is not None:
        return metrics['signal'] - metrics['noise']
    elif metrics['signal'] is not None:
        return metrics['signal'] + 90
    return None

def monitor(interface, model=None):
    smoothed_snr = None
    print(f"{'Time':<8} | {'Signal':>7} | {'SNR':>6} | {'Status':<25}")
    print("-" * 50)
    try:
        while True:
            timestamp = time.strftime("%H:%M:%S")
            metrics = get_wireless_metrics(interface)
            snr = calculate_snr(metrics)
            if snr is not None:
                smoothed_snr = snr if smoothed_snr is None else SMOOTHING_FACTOR * smoothed_snr + (1 - SMOOTHING_FACTOR) * snr
            signal_str = f"{metrics['signal']} dBm" if metrics['signal'] is not None else "N/A"
            snr_str = f"{smoothed_snr:.1f} dB" if smoothed_snr is not None else "N/A"
            status = "NO SIGNAL"
            if snr is not None:
                if model:
                    features = [[metrics['signal'] or -100, metrics['noise'] or -90, smoothed_snr or 0]]
                    pred = model.predict(features)[0]
                    status = f"{pred:.1f} cm" if isinstance(pred, float) else pred
                else:
                    status = ("VERY CLOSE" if smoothed_snr < 26 else
                              "NORMAL RANGE" if smoothed_snr < 33 else
                              "MOVING AWAY" if smoothed_snr < 40 else
                              "FAR AWAY")
            print(f"{timestamp:<8} | {signal_str:>7} | {snr_str:>6} | {status:<25}", end="\r")
            time.sleep(SAMPLING_RATE)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("\nMonitoring stopped.")

This code is robust, with fallbacks for metric extraction and support for both static and ML-based detection. Hackers can extend it to log data to a remote server or trigger scripts on proximity events.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• OS: Linux (Kali, Ubuntu, etc.) with a Wi-Fi adapter (monitor mode not required but useful).
  • Software: Python 3.6+, scikit-learn, joblib, numpy.
  • Tools: iw, iwconfig, and read access to /proc/net/wireless.

Install dependencies:

sudo apt install python3-{sklearn,joblib,numpy}

Check your Wi-Fi interface:

ip link show

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
• Monitor Mode: 

    python3 wifi_proximity.py --interface wlan0
    Uses wifi_proximity_model.pkl if present; falls back to static thresholds.

  • Data Collection Mode: 

    python3 wifi_proximity.py --collect --interface wlan0
    Input distances (cm) or labels (e.g., "VERY CLOSE"). Saves to wifi_prox_data.csv.

  • Model Training Mode: 

    python3 wifi_proximity.py --train
    Trains and saves the model to wifi_proximity_model.pkl.

docs.title: Sample Output
docs.text:
Monitoring output looks like:

Time     | Signal  | SNR    | Status
------------------------------------------------
12:34:56 | -50 dBm | 40.0 dB | FAR AWAY
12:34:57 | -48 dBm | 42.0 dB | FAR AWAY

With an ML model, you might see distances (e.g., "150.2 cm") for regression.

docs.title: Hacking Tips and Tricks
docs.text:
• Spoofing Defense: Wi-Fi signals can be manipulated (e.g., via signal amplifiers). Train models in the target environment to detect anomalies in SNR patterns.
  • Stealth Mode: Run in a Docker container or Raspberry Pi for covert deployment. Redirect output to a log file or C2 server with tee or nc.
  • Model Evasion: Test model robustness by introducing noise (e.g., using aircrack-ng to simulate interference). Retrain with adversarial data to harden the model.
  • Integration: Pipe proximity events to metasploit or nmap scripts for automated pentesting workflows.
  • Hardware Mods: Use high-gain antennas to extend range or directional antennas for precise tracking.

docs.title: Challenges and Limitations
docs.text:
• Signal Noise: Multipath effects, walls, and interference can skew SNR. Train models with diverse data to compensate.
  • Hardware Variability: Some adapters don’t report noise, forcing reliance on the fallback SNR formula. Test on target hardware.
  • ML Dependence: Model accuracy hinges on training data quality. Collect data in realistic conditions (e.g., during a recon phase).
  • Latency: The 0.5s sampling rate may miss rapid movements. Tune SAMPLING_RATE for faster response at the cost of stability.

docs.title: Future Enhancements for Pentesters
docs.text:
• Multi-Adapter Support: Combine multiple Wi-Fi interfaces for triangulation or redundancy.
  • Packet Injection: Integrate with scapy to correlate proximity with specific devices (MAC addresses).
  • C2 Integration: Stream data to a command-and-control server for remote monitoring.
  • ML Upgrades: Swap LinearRegression/SVC for XGBoost or neural nets for better accuracy.
  • Web Dashboard: Build a Flask-based UI for real-time visualization during engagements.

docs.text:
